more_beautiful.reason: B looks finished and well made: a warm paper, rust and green palette, Rockwell slab headings, custom repair icons and a rotated manila tag. A is a plain yellow-and-black form page whose yellow bands stop short of the edges at desktop width while the grey footer runs full width, and its hero has dashed placeholder boxes.

less_generic.reason: B's manila repair tag carrying the live date, the matching tag favicon, the stitched wordmark and the repair-specific copy ('dodgy switches', 'crumbs out of the toaster') mark it as this repair cafe, even though its eyebrow, two-tone headline and icon-card/3-step skeleton is a familiar AI landing-page pattern. A's bare yellow bands and GOV.UK-style form could belong to any organisation.

better_overall.reason: B is good enough to publish and more complete: how it works, an own-risk note, access needs, and a sturdy booking flow with a copy-and-phone fallback and a warning to organisers while the address is still a placeholder. A is more honest and very accessible, but it looks unfinished and, as shipped, its booking email opens with no recipient.

A: The next date is the H1 and is calculated automatically: it shows 'Tomorrow' and the two Saturdays after it, and dates can be cancelled from one list.

The form is as accessible as a GOV.UK one: large radio cards with visible radios, an error summary with links, inline errors, aria-invalid/describedby, focus handling, an 'Error:' title prefix, and prefers-contrast/forced-colors support.
Very honest: missing hall, email and phone are marked as explicit '[... to add]' placeholders, and the copy stays close to the brief.
Easy to read for older visitors: 18px body text and near-black on yellow at high contrast.
Visitors see a review 'tag' summarising the booking before they send it; phone is optional and there is no redundant email field.
B: Warm, consistent identity without inventing a logo: a type-only wordmark with a dashed 'stitch' underline, a manila luggage-tag hero showing the live next date, a matching favicon and hand-drawn repair icons.
Content visitors can use: can/can't-fix lists with reasons, 'How it works' (bring it clean, fix it together), an own-risk note, access needs, a call for volunteers and an 'Open in Maps' link.

Sturdy booking: dynamic dates, large time chips and icon chips for the item, email or phone required, inline errors with focus, a honeypot, an optional form-service endpoint, and a mailto with a copy-to-clipboard and phone fallback. 'Book another item' keeps the contact details.
A note to organisers appears while bookings still go to example.org, and the page still works without JavaScript.
Adapts well to phones; the booking intro stays in view on desktop; it has a skip link and print styles.

A: As shipped, the booking mailto has no recipient. bookingEmail() only reads an <a href='mailto:'>, but the footer holds a placeholder span. Typing an address into that span still won't fix it, nothing warns the owner, and there is no fallback if the email app doesn't open.
Looks unfinished: no header or wordmark treatment, dashed placeholder boxes in the hero, and yellow bands inset 80px at desktop width while the footer runs full width.
The yellow-ringed bullets in 'What we can fix' look like radio buttons, which is confusing directly above a form full of radios.
Austere and civic in tone: there is no sense of community and nothing for first-timers about what happens on the day.
The 'Check booking' button label is ambiguous (it sounds like checking availability), and the Avenir Next look only appears on Apple devices.
B: Invents specifics the owner never gave: kettles, hairdryers, radios, fans and soft toys; no phones or laptops; one item per booking; booked visitors seen first. The owner has to review all of these.

Placeholders that look real ('The Church Hall, Church Street, Your Town AB1 2CD', the fictional 01632 960123 number, example.org) appear as facts in the hero tag and footer. Only the email triggers a warning, and 'Open in Maps' searches a fake address.

The page skeleton is a familiar AI landing pattern (uppercase eyebrow, two-tone slogan headline, pill CTA plus arrow link, icon-tile cards, numbered step cards, tick checklist, dark three-column footer), and cream with terracotta and serif headings is now a common AI look.
The page is long on mobile (about 7,600px), and the tag pushes the intro text and main CTA below the first screen.
If the owner forgets to edit, the organiser note is visible to the public; 24-hour slot labels are a little less friendly than '10am' or 'Midday'.
